1973 Plymouth Duster 340 Six-Pack Is the One-of-Zero Hero Chrysler Never Had the Brass To Build
19 photos
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER
When gearheads discuss high-profile classic Mopar machines, names like Hemi winged warriors, the twin-cousin E-bodies Cuda and Challenger, Max Wedge Polaras and Savoys, letter car Chryslers, Crown Imperials, and De Soto Adventurers usually kickstart the conversation. The Plymouth Duster rarely enters this chat – but when it does, it slams the doors open with the force of a category Six hurricane. As in Six Barrels.
To set the record straight, we are not talking about standard grocery-getter models. The Duster 340 earned a reputation as a big-block slayer on streets and drag strips, unafraid to take on game much larger than itself.
A restored 1973 Plymouth Duster 340 surfaced at a classic car cruise night in San Diego, California, captured on the CARFINDER YouTube channel. While this Plymouth left the factory with a 340 V8, the owner added an upward deviation from factory specifications. The video highlights a six-barrel carburetor setup, an induction system Plymouth never officially offered on the entire 1973 Duster factory model lineup. Or on any Duster, period. Or on any other car post-1971.
To fit this induction setup, the owner installed a custom hood scoop, and retrofitted drag wheels for good measure – and good intentions. This six-barrel setup bridges the gap to the history of the Chrysler 340 V8. This powerhouse debuted in 1968 as a high-performance engine designed for high revolutions (pun intended).
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER Chrysler engineered it from the ground up to rival the Chevrolet 350 and 302. The standard 4-barrel variant produced 275 horsepower, but Chrysler conservatively underrated these factory output power numbers.
The six-barrel variant of this engine achieved historical status. The 340 V8 received three two-barrel carburetors for the 1970 model year, a setup was introduced to meet homologation requirements for SCCA Trans-Am racing. Chrysler bolted this induction system onto modified engine blocks featuring thicker webs, unleashing 290 horsepower and 345 pound-feet of torque. The NHRA rated this engine much higher, placing it in the 320 to 330 horsepower racing class.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER This six-barrel configuration found its way into only two cars. Dodge received it for the Challenger T/A, and Plymouth fitted it to the AAR Cuda. Production numbers were limited, with 2,399 units built for the Challenger T/A and 2,724 units for the AAR Cuda. By 1971, the six-barrel setup vanished. The standard four-barrel 340 powered Chrysler products until it went out of production after the 1973 model year concluded.
Federal emissions regulations and lowered compression ratios sapped the engine of its power. Plymouth replaced the 340 with the larger 360 V8 in 1974. The 360 offered more torque but lacked the high-revving soul of its predecessor. The 1973 Duster 340 represented the final chapter for this engine.
The Plymouth Duster itself has a documented history, with production spanning continuously from 1970 through 1976. It remained a single generation vehicle platform, introduced to replace the A-body Valiant, and to fill the void left in the segment by the Barracuda’s promotion to the E-body platform.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The Duster was built upon the Valiant compact platform – in fact, at its birth, it was dubbed Valiant Duster, for one year only. Plymouth designers received a budget of 15,000,000 dollars to create a different exterior look.
They retained the Valiant front end and crafted a semi-fastback rear. Enthusiasts cite 1970 as the best year of production for the Duster. This inaugural year introduced the factory visual expression of the car, free from crash bumpers that plagued later production model year body design iterations.
The engines and transmissions available that year offered something for every buyer. Economy drivers opted for the 198 cubic-inch or 225 cubic-inch Slant Sixes. Drivers seeking more vigor chose the 318 V8 or gravitated toward the top-tier 340 V8. Buyers paired these powerplants with a 3-speed manual, a 4-speed manual, or a 3-speed Torqueflite automatic transmission . Competitive base pricing proved to be the key to the overall sales success story.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The factory base price for the cheapest 1970 Duster with the inline 6 was 2,172 dollars. The 340 model began at 2,547 dollars. Adding the Torqueflite automatic transmission increased the base price for a 340 automatic to 2,760 dollars. This affordability allowed Plymouth to sell 217,192 units in 1970. In 1971, production hit 186,478 units. By 1972, it surged to 228,022 units. The Duster remained a sales juggernaut during the 1973 model year.
Plymouth sold 248,105 Dusters in 1973. Out of those, 15,731 were Duster 340 models, out of the total production for Chrysler vehicles equipped with the 340 V8 of 51,067 units. This was the second-best year for the engine, trailing the 56,672 record achieved in 1970. Most of the 340 models sold in 1973 were automatics, with 8,312 receiving a Torqueflite. Just 2,037 models featured a 4-speed manual gearbox.
The standard 3-speed manual transmission came in 1,492 examples. The math doesn’t add up, does it (pun premeditated)? The total “shipped to US dealers” Duster 340s went as high as 11,841 units – according to Galen Govier’s White Book.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The reliable Torqueflite automatic was the preferred choice for drag racing, which brings us back to the green 1973 Duster captured by CARFINDER, a tribute to Mopar history. The owner did not stick to factory specifications, choosing to graft the six-barrel setup onto the A-body. This created a lightweight machine that Chrysler never built, righting a historical wrong done over half a century ago.
Since the owner was absent when the video was filmed, the exact power output remains unknown. The large hood scoop and the wide rear tires suggest the vehicle frequents the quarter-mile. A well-tuned Duster 340 could embarrass big-block cars at the stoplight drags due to its lightweight chassis. It weighed significantly less than a GTO or a Challenger R/T, operating as the ultimate street-sleeper nose-bleeder.
